They had plenty of data the protagonist didn't need to die." No. Wrong. The protagonist was the first person with immunity, they didn't have any other kids. And people who understood the disease said that they needed her brain tissue to develop a cure. I understand that questioning the expertise of scientists is part and parcel for the terminally stupid but this is a fictional disease in a fictional world. If the writer says "that's the only way to make a cure" then that's the only way to make a cure. The protagonist ends the game lying to the protagonist to try to make her feel good and she is smart enough to know he is lying. The last shot of that game is her looking disappointed and worried not grateful.

The haters of the game expect things from video games: they expect to feel powerful, triumphant, to make a difference in the world, and to feel like a hero. The game has never really been about because the wider industry does cater to those feelings. When the protagonist died in the sequel they got angry because he didn't die like a hero, so they felt like the game had messed up, that it was doing it wrong. This is also why I see comparisons to that controversial movie and "the game was badly subverting expectations". That argument implies the developer set out to subvert expectations. I would argue the game's marketing did no such thing, it was painfully clear that the protagonist would die, that the younger character would be the starring character, and that the game would be dark.
I'm chalking it up to a combination of not paying attention while playing the game, taking the character's lie at face value, and then some Mandela effect style group think memory alteration.
